strategy.summary: Small founder-owned CNC shop (35 staff, sound finances) and the 100% source for flange part:320030 under framework ctr:4600070220. It is fully booked (news:20260320-04), will not confirm our rising forecast and says it will favour firm long-term commitments (doc:20260915-70220-P09). It has also asked for faster payment (doc:20260511-70220-M1). Price has been flat since 2024, and our should-cost (cost:320030) puts the price only about 4% above cost with no margin included. Bar steel and labour drivers point upward. The second source's new quote is dearer (quote:7200009). Its delivery and quality are poor, but we pay late almost every time. Leverage leans to them: secure capacity with commitment, length and cash rather than squeezing price. Evidence covers one part and the should-cost is low-confidence.
strategy.decision_maker: Most likely the founder-owners (Obermaier/Huber); no named decision-maker is recorded. The new inside-sales contact (doc:20251207-70220-N) probably relays to them, and evidence on this is thin.

persona.style: pragmatic, relationship-driven, modest asks that historically settle low; now confident because fully booked
other_traits: thin margin vs should-cost despite trait list

needs.detail: Wants firm, long-term binding commitments before allocating scarce capacity to us.
Asked for 10-day payment against a cash discount. Our late payment (8 days on average) is a grievance.
Price has been flat since 2024 while bar and labour costs rose. It will seek a 2027 increase or protection on bar steel.
Called Hollerau an important reference customer.

constraints.detail: Backlog of more than six months and no new projects. It cannot confirm our full forecast, and lead times are stretched beyond 35 days.
Explicitly prioritises customers with firm long-term commitments.
Price is fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice 90 days before year-end. This binds them, and it also protects them once a price is agreed.
100% quota. Hrvelec is qualified at 0% quota, quoted higher, with a longer lead time from CZ. We own the tooling.
Margin is thin: price is about 4% above a no-margin should-cost, within that estimate's error band.

Answers its own request for faster payment; a cheap way to buy price or capacity.
Reminds it of its own reference-customer statement; supports a partnership framing.
Use only to cap an increase: the price already covers cost. Do not use it to demand a cut.
Bar prices are off their peak, which tempers a steel-based ask.
Small checkable offset on power; a fresh-fact filler.
History of settling well below its ask; supports holding increases small.
Use only if it seeks a 2027 change without timely notice.
Above-peer ppm; a factual counter to any premium-for-service claim. State it neutrally.
Weak on-time delivery; pair it with a request for a capacity confirmation, not with a price demand.

trades.why: Long commitment is what it rewards with capacity; 24 months captures the value.
A binding volume within our forecast secures priority allocation.
It asked for fast payment; trade it for a price step or capacity, ideally in the final round.
Accepting its realistic lead time costs us little and eases a full shop; short lead times would be priced steeply.
Fallback if it pushes hard on bar steel: a bar-index clause with a modest weight instead of a large step. Price the risk first, as the index is rising.
Tie quality improvement to the commitment package.

price_view.reasoning: The price sits about 4% above a no-margin should-cost and has been flat for three years while drivers rose by several percent. The rival quote is dearer even before freight. Realistic goal: limit an increase to well below its ask, buying it down with length, binding volume and fast payment rather than demanding a cut.

do: Acknowledge its capacity situation and its request for faster payment
Frame the deal as a long-term partnership with a reference customer
Offer concrete binding commitments in a single clean sheet
Commit to paying on time going forward
dont: Threaten to move the tooling or switch to the Czech source
Lecture on delivery and quality as a price weapon
Ask open questions about its cost structure
Demand shorter lead times or long payment terms

traps: Citing the rival quote: it is dearer than the current price and backfires
Using should-cost to demand a cut from a capacity-full supplier gets dismissed as theoretical and risks deprioritisation
Exit threats via the termination clause or tooling ownership: it is sound and fully booked, and can simply walk
Hammering on its delivery and quality while we pay nearly every invoice late invites a late-payment counter
Citing market news (copper, electronics) or non-checkable index-peak arguments
Asking 60-90 payment days from a supplier that wants cash
strategy.writer_notes: Lead with commitment: binding volume, a longer contract and faster payment, in exchange for a confirmed capacity allocation and a minimal or zero price step. Accept its own lead time. Hold should-cost and the bar-index easing for later rounds to cap any increase. Keep the tone warm and mention its reference-customer remark. Keep the CZ source as quiet background, never as a threat. If it insists on bar-steel pass-through, consider an index clause at a modest weight. Confirm our accounts payable will pay on time before offering fast payment.

findings.text: Price EUR 16.02 sits only about +4.0% above our bottom-up should-cost of EUR 15.40, which includes no margin. Its margin is therefore thin, roughly 4%, and within the estimate's ~5% error. There is little or no room to push below 16.02 without leaving it under a healthy margin.

The cost drivers argue for an increase, not a cut. Over 12 months, cold-drawn bars (PPI-C2431, weight 0.32) rose +12.3%, about +3.9% on the price. Labour (LCI-C, 0.33) rose +2.7%, about +0.9%. Power (0.02) fell -3.7%, worth only -0.07%. The weighted effect is about +4.7%. The only offsets are small: bars are -2.3% off their June 2026 peak and power is down.

The price has been flat at 16.02 since 2024, after a -4.1% cut from 16.71 in 2023. Meanwhile bar and labour costs have risen. Its last ask (+3.5%, Dec 2025) settled at 0%. Pressure is building, so expect a case for roughly +3.5–5%.

Benchmarks: in Apr 2025 it quoted 17.30 against Hrvelec's 13.90. Hrvelec's Sep 2026 quote of 16.33 FCA is +1.9% above the current price, before freight from CZ. The second source no longer undercuts, so 16.02 looks at or below market.
The should-cost confidence is only 5% and it rests on a single part, so the economic evidence is thin. Steel news (+7.3% since January) supports its side.

findings.text: Small founder-owned shop (35 staff, turnover 2-5 M EUR). Decisions most likely sit with the owners (Obermaier/Huber), with no long approval ladder. Finances are sound and stable (equity 31.1%, credit index 245, unchanged in 12 months). There is no distress, so it can afford to walk away. Evidence on who decides is thin: no named decision-maker is recorded.

Capacity is the key issue. The supplier has been fully booked since March 2026 (backlog over 6 months, no new projects). On 2026-09-15 it declined to confirm our full forecast for part:320030, said lead times are longer than agreed, and said it will prioritise customers with firm long-term commitments. This is a red flag that we are being deprioritised, and it signals the trade they want: binding volume and a longer contract.

The supplier values cash. It asked us to pay within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount. Our payment record gives it a grievance: 94.4% of invoices paid late, 8.1 days late on average, up to 17 days, and no discount ever taken. Faster, reliable payment is a cheap concession we can trade, but expect them to raise our late payment if we push hard.

Relationship and recognition matter to them. At our supplier day they called Hollerau an important reference customer. The relationship is long (supplier since 2007, part approved since 2013, 100% quota). Our spend is only about 4.4% of their turnover, so the reference value may matter more to them than the volume.

Their performance weakens their position. On-time delivery is 56% against the requested date versus a 95% target and a peer median of 84.6%, and it is falling. Quality is 731 ppm versus a peer median of 457, with 7 complaints on part:320030 and one 8D still open.
The sales contact changed to a new inside-sales colleague. That person probably has limited authority, so concessions likely need owner sign-off.

findings.text: Framework agreement ctr:4600070220 covers only part:320030 (flange DN 65 PN 16), runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice, so notice is due by 2027-04-01. That exit is still open and credible.
Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end (by about 2026-10-02 for 2027). A price increase notified later has no contractual basis for 2027.
Payment is 30 days net against our 60-day standard, so it is already a concession to them. Incoterm is EXW, which puts freight on us. Lead time is 35 days.

Quality agreement terms: 95% on-time target and EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint. Actual performance is far below this: 56% on time against requested date (76% against confirmed) and 731 ppm against a peer median of 457.

Renewal history shows the supplier asks little and settles low: asked -0.4% and settled -4.1% (2024), asked +3.1% and settled 0 (2025), asked +3.5% and settled 0 (2026). Average gap is about 3.4 pp, and the price has been flat at 16.02 since 2024.

Mutual dependency: the supplier holds a 100% quota, but we own the tooling and sup:70240 (CZ) is qualified at 0% quota. A second-source RFQ (rfq:6000000209, 15,600 pcs/yr) has been quoted, with the rival at 16.33 FCA, +1.9% above the current price. Our spend is about 4.4% of their turnover.

Counterweight on their side: the supplier is fully booked, cannot confirm our forecast and says it will prioritise firm long-term commitments. It is financially sound, so it can walk away. Two further asks for them: it wants faster payment, and we pay 8 days late on average.

arguments.text: Price has been frozen at 16.02 since January 2024, after we gave a 4.1% cut in the 2024 renewal. We asked for 3.1% and 3.5% in the last two renewals and settled at 0 both times. Meanwhile cold-drawn bar is up 12.3% in 12 months and labour is up 2.7%. Together those two drivers are about 65% of our cost.

Hollerau's own competitive check confirms our price is fair. Hrvelec quoted 16.33 FCA CZ in September 2026, which is above our 16.02 before freight, with a 42-day lead time and only a 90-day validity. Moving the part away would cost Hollerau more.

We are fully booked: a backlog of more than six months and no new projects accepted. Capacity is scarce, and we will give it to customers who commit firmly and for the long term. Hollerau's forecast is rising (10,780 pcs for the next 12 months against 9,520 ordered), so Hollerau needs our capacity more than before.
Hollerau's own should-cost puts 16.02 only about 4% above cost with no margin included. There is no room for a cut; if anything, the numbers show we are working near break-even.

Hollerau pays late on almost every invoice: 94.4% paid late, 8.1 days past due on average. That is effectively free credit. We asked in May for 10-day payment against a cash discount and still have no answer.
Quality is improving: ppm fell from about 1,200 to 626–731 in the last two scorecards, and we have no overdue 8D reports.

weak_points: Delivery is poor. Only 56% on time to the requested date in the last 12 months, 40% late, about 18 days late on average. The scorecard has been amber for every quarter on record.
We have had 23 supplier-caused complaints since late 2023, with recurring defects (missing marking, leakage, burrs), and qn:20005010 is still open without an 8D close.
We would not confirm the forecast even though the frame contract specifies a 35-day lead time. Rush order po:4500014340-10 was confirmed two weeks late.
The 90-day notice in clause 3.1 means an increase for 2027 should have been notified by about 2 October. If we miss that date, the price is fixed for 2027 under ctr:4600070220#3.1.
The should-cost confidence is only 5% and does not support a loss claim with hard numbers. Power prices are down 3.7% (-43% against 2022).
In the 2025 RFQ Hrvelec was much cheaper (13.9). They are qualified, and Hollerau owns the tooling, so switching is technically easy.
Copper and electronics price rises are not relevant to us; I should not cite them.
wants: A firm commitment of about 10,000–11,000 pcs per year over 24–36 months (extend the frame to 2028/29), in return for a moderate increase or holding near the current price.
Payment in 10 days (cash discount about 2%), or at least strict 30 days net.
An index clause on bar steel (PPI-C2431, about 32% weight) instead of a high fixed increase.
A realistic lead time of 42–49 days in the contract.
Effective date of 1 January 2027; frozen per year as before.
Lower chargeback, or no increase to the 150 EUR flat fee.
red_lines: No firm confirmation of the full forecast volume without a binding commitment.
No 35-day lead time with penalties while we are fully booked.
Not below 16.02 unless payment is within 10 days and the volume is bound over 3 years; ideally at least +3%.
I do not want a stricter ppm or penalty regime without a price adjustment.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau as an important reference customer. Point out three years at an unchanged price after our 2024 cut, bar steel +12.3% and labour +2.7%. Ask for +5.5% (about 16.90) from 1 January 2027, with a fixed price for 2027. As an alternative, offer about +3% with a bar-steel index clause and a binding 24–36-month volume. In return, we reserve capacity for the forecast and confirm a 42-day lead time. Repeat the request for 10-day payment against a discount.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that the price has been stable while bar and labour costs rose, and we value that you held it. To keep it in proportion: weighted by their share of the part, those drivers support a modest step, well below the asks you have made before, and bar prices have already eased from their recent peak while power has fallen. Our renewals have consistently settled well below the ask, and the contract fixes prices per calendar year, so any change has to follow its notice rule. We would rather answer real cost pressure with commitment, length and faster payment than with a large price step.

We agree the current price is competitive, and that is one reason we want to keep working with you. A benchmark showing your price is fair supports keeping it stable; it does not justify a rise. We also look at total cost, which includes delivery reliability and quality, and on both your record leaves room for improvement. The earlier benchmark showed the market can be keener than today's single quote.

We understand that your shop is full and that firm commitments earn priority, and we are prepared to give exactly that. We can offer a longer term and a binding annual volume within our shared forecast. In return we need a confirmed capacity allocation and delivery at the lead time we agree. Our rising volume is also more business for you on a part you already run, and you described us as an important reference customer.

We are not asking for a cut, and we do not want to push you below a healthy margin. The same estimate says the current price already covers your cost. That supports a small, careful adjustment at most, not a large one. The commitments we offer, a longer term, binding volume and faster cash, lower your cost and risk, which is the right way to protect margin.

That is fair criticism, and we apologise that your request was left unanswered. We will make sure our invoices are paid on time from now on. We are also open to a short payment term with a cash discount as part of the overall package, so it improves your cash flow and is reflected in the price.

The rolling level is still above what comparable suppliers achieve, and the same defect types keep recurring on this part, with one complaint still not closed. We would like to lock the progress in with a quality commitment as part of the longer agreement.

press: We would welcome a firm monthly capacity confirmation, since on-time delivery against our requested dates has stayed well below the target in our quality agreement.
As our framework sets a standard lead time, we would like to agree a realistic lead time you can reliably confirm, so that rush orders are no longer confirmed late.
Under the price clause of our framework, prices are fixed per calendar year, so we would like to agree any change within the notice terms it sets out.
Power, which is part of your cost base, has become cheaper over the last year, and we think this belongs in a balanced view of cost drivers.

arguments.note: ctr:4600070220#3.1 (price): Prices as per the price annex, fixed for each calendar year. Changes require written notice of at least 90 days before the end of the calendar year.

arguments.sentence: Our framework agreement sets the payment terms.
arguments.note: ctr:4600070220#4.1 (payment): Payment: 30 days net. Our standard is 60 days; shorter terms are its benefit.

arguments.sentence: Our framework agreement sets the delivery terms and the standard lead time.
arguments.note: ctr:4600070220#5.1 (delivery): Delivery EXW; standard lead time 35 days from order.

arguments.sentence: Our framework agreement includes the quality agreement with its delivery target.
arguments.note: ctr:4600070220#6.1 (quality): The quality agreement applies: on-time delivery target 95 %, flat fee of EUR 150 per supplier-caused complaint.

arguments.sentence: Our framework agreement renews only unless either side gives notice.
arguments.note: ctr:4600070220#8.1 (term): Valid from 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30; extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice. To stop the renewal, notice by 2027-04-01 (still open: a credible exit).
